**Abstract- Previous research found that most people live in areas where accurate air quality measurements are not readily accessible. With a premature death rate of about 7 million, wearable air quality monitoring devices are an emerging technology that has increased in popularity in the last decade. However, the calibration required for accurate measurements is often not feasible in a dynamic, real-life environment. Through the creation of a wearable edge AI calibrated air quality monitoring device, Sensa, an increased accuracy compared to state-of-the-art competitors will be available to the public, benefiting public safety.**

I. INTRODUCTION

Air pollution is one of the most widespread environmental challenges today, and it directly impacts human health on a global scale. Poor air quality can cause respiratory and cardiovascular problems, especially in people who live or work in polluted environments. While there are stationary air-quality monitoring systems available, they are often expensive, complex, and not easily accessible to individuals who want to track the air around them on a daily basis. Our project aims to address this problem by developing a wearable air-quality monitoring device that measures particulate matter and gases in real time. The device integrates low-cost sensors with an embedded machine learning model to automatically interpret air-quality data and determine the user's level of exposure. This information is then sent to a smartphone or computer for easy tracking and visualization.

Recent developments in environmental sensing emphasize the growing need for portable solutions capable of matching the precision of laboratory systems while maintaining low power consumption and affordability. Studies demonstrate that fine particulate matter (PM2.5) remains one of the most critical pollutants affecting global health, with over 99% of the world's population exposed to unsafe levels and approximately seven million premature deaths each year attributed to poor air quality \[9\], \[10\].

To strengthen the academic context of this report, two journal papers help provide better insight to the topic. Kim and Moon's review of machine-learning-based quality control for low-cost air-quality monitoring highlights persistent issues including calibration drift, environmental cross-sensitivity, and dependence on cloud processing, which limit the reliability of portable sensors \[12\]. Similarly, Tarin-Carrasco et al. demonstrate the significant health impact of fine particulate matter exposures and emphasize the need for accurate personal-level monitoring tools aligned with long-term health outcomes \[9\] \[10\]. These works collectively reveal a clear research gap: existing low-cost and wearable sensors lack stable, autonomous calibration methods capable of maintaining accuracy under real world variability.

Our project directly addresses this gap by integrating an embedded AI calibration model, executed locally on the ESP32-S3, capable of correcting drift and environmental variation without cloud support. Unlike existing commercial devices, the proposed wearable conducts continuous on-device inference, enabling mobility, low latency, and privacy while matching the accuracy of higher-grade equipment. In doing so, this project advances the field toward reliable, affordable, and real-time personal exposure monitoring.

_A. What is the Purpose?_

The main goal of this project is to create a portable, affordable, and reliable solution that empowers users to understand their environment and make informed decisions about their health and safety. By combining compact hardware, wireless connectivity, and on-device AI, our design provides a more personal and accessible way to monitor air quality - without relying on external calibration or cloud processing. Similar edge-deployed sensing systems have shown that integrating lightweight machine learning on-device significantly improves responsiveness and

reliability, especially when cloud connectivity is limited \[15\]. Ultimately, this project demonstrates how embedded systems and machine learning can be combined to solve real-world problems. The wearable air-quality monitor bridges the gap between environmental awareness and personal health technology, offering a practical tool that helps users stay informed and protected wherever they go.

_B. What Makes This Product Different?_

Most wearable sensors are expensive, require frequent manual calibration, and often rely on external reference stations to maintain accuracy before deployment \[5\]. In contrast, the SEN55 leverages on-device AI to automate calibration, enabling faster and more reliable performance in dynamic environments. Integrating a trained AI model will enable the device to assess the air quality, collect data, and make predictions of future pollutant levels based on observed environmental patterns. Predictive analytics using embedded AI has been shown to improve temporal accuracy by forecasting near-future pollutant concentration trends based on environmental differentials and previous readings, as demonstrated in Bindhu et al. \[6\] and Koziel et al. \[12\]

II. RELATED WORKS

Air-quality sensing technology has advanced rapidly over the past decade, with a growing variety of commercially available products targeting both professional and consumer markets \[6\]. Despite this progress, significant challenges remain, including sensor calibration drift, cross-sensitivity, and inconsistent data reliability under changing environmental conditions \[5\], \[12\]. Most portable monitors provide minute-by-minute readings; however, these short-term measurements may not align with existing health exposure standards, which are typically based on much longer durations-from several hours to years \[13\]. For example, the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) defines exposure limits such as the Permissible Exposure Limit (PEL), an 8-hour time-weighted average, and the Short-Term Exposure Limit (STEL), a 15-minute average \[13\]. These regulatory benchmarks highlight the difficulty of interpreting short-interval data in the context of long-term health outcomes.

Moreover, in a holistic view of the exposome-the totality of environmental exposures across an individual's lifespan-it is increasingly recognized that indoor, outdoor, and occupational exposures should not be treated as isolated domains but rather as interconnected aspects of overall air-quality impact \[13\]. Recent evaluations of low-cost PM and VOC sensors have shown that while affordability and accessibility have improved, reliability and calibration stability still lag behind industrial-grade equipment \[5\], \[6\]. Commercial wearable devices such as Atmotube and Flow depend on centralized databases or periodic cloud recalibration, which limits real-time responsiveness and raises privacy concerns.

To overcome these limitations, emerging research has focused on AI-driven calibration methods that enable self-correcting, adaptive performance at the edge. Studies such as Narayana et al. \[4\] demonstrate that advanced machine-learning models like EEATC outperform traditional linear regression in dynamic conditions, while Zimmerman et al. \[20\] and Smith et al. \[19\] show that random forest and ensemble-based calibration significantly improve low-cost sensor accuracy. These findings motivate our approach-embedding adaptive calibration intelligence directly within the wearable hardware-to achieve both independence from external systems and greater measurement accuracy in real time.

III. FUNCTIONAL DECOMPOSITION

_A. Level 0 Functional Decomposition_

At the highest level, the system functions as a black box that receives environmental measurements and outputs an air-quality classification. The Level 0 function is therefore:

Input: PM measurement 🡪 System function: Determine PM size and pollutant severity 🡪 Output: Air-quality level

_B. Level 1 Functional Decomposition_

Level 1 expands the primary function into major sub-functions:

Filter sensor noise 🡪 Extract features 🡪 Prune and validate data 🡪 perform regression and train calibration model 🡪 Classify air quality 🡪 Communicate classification to user

These functions collectively transform raw SEN55 data into a calibrated and interpretable exposure classification, supporting real-time feedback in dynamic environments.

IV. SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE

The system architecture integrates the SEN55 environmental sensor, ESP32-S3 microcontroller, Li-ion battery subsystem, BLE/Wi-Fi communication modules, TinyML calibration models, and a lightweight user-notification interface. Sensor data flows from the SEN55 to the ESP32-S3 over I²C, where the microcontroller performs noise filtering, feature extraction, model inference, and threshold evaluation. The TinyML model corrects for thermal drift, humidity variation, and sensor aging, following methods described in prior research \[3\], \[11\], \[12\]. The ESP32-S3 manages power by entering periodic sleep cycles while maintaining one-minute sampling intervals, consistent with validated practices \[4\], \[13\]. Processed results are transmitted via BLE or Wi-Fi to a smartphone interface, while onboard LEDs provide immediate exposure cues. The architecture prioritizes low power consumption, real-time operation, and independence from cloud computation, ensuring reliability across mobile and stationary use cases.

V. CUSTOMER REQUIREMENTS

_A. Who is it for?_

The wearable air-quality monitor is designed for individuals who want to better understand and manage their exposure to harmful environmental conditions. Our target users include people who are regularly exposed to varying air-quality levels and need a simple, reliable way to track their surroundings. This group includes urban commuters, industrial and construction workers, laboratory researchers, and health-conscious individuals who want air-quality feed-back throughout the day.

_B. Price_

The wearable air-quality monitor is designed to remain affordable, with a target price under one hundred dollars to ensure accessibility for a broad range of users. By using cost-effective components without compromising precision or reliability, the product appeals to students, commuters, and professionals alike. Its affordability addresses a key gap in the market where most portable monitors are prohibitively expensive or limited in function.

_C. Quality_

Customers expect dependable, accurate readings over long periods. The device's self-calibrating AI ensures consistent performance and minimizes sensor drift, a common issue in low-cost systems. By applying ML-based correction methods supported by recent studies \[4\], \[5\], \[11\], the product maintains high-quality measurements in both indoor and outdoor environments.

_D. Functionality_

The monitor measures particulate matter (PM), volatile organic compounds (VOC), temperature, and humidity in real time. It connects seamlessly to smartphones or computers to display live and historical data, and provides visual or auditory alerts when pollutant levels become hazardous. Real-time BLE/Wi-Fi communication aligns with IoT trends in environmental monitoring, allowing for continuous awareness and potential integration with public mapping systems \[6\].

_E. Reliability_

Reliability is central to the monitor's design. The AI-driven system automatically calibrates sensors to correct drift, ensuring continuous accuracy. Users can depend on consistent readings whether indoors, outdoors, or on the move, fostering trust in the data and supporting daily health and safety decisions.

_F. Performance_

Performance expectations include precise, real-time air-quality readings, full workday battery life (12+ hours), and lightweight comfort for daily wear. The device's local processing eliminates dependence on cloud systems, reducing latency and protecting user privacy. These features directly address performance limitations found in existing IoT-based monitors \[6\].

_G. Sustainability_

Sustainability is built into the product through the use of rechargeable lithium-ion batteries, durable materials, and long sensor lifespan. By minimizing electronic waste and extending product longevity, the monitor promotes environmental responsibility while reducing the need for frequent replacements or disposables.

_H. Convenience_

Designed for everyday use, the monitor requires minimal setup and maintenance. It operates autonomously, displaying clear results through a simple app or visual indicators. Compact and comfortable, it fits easily into the user's daily routine, providing valuable air-quality data without adding inconvenience.

_I. Efficiency_

Efficiency is reflected in the device's ability to collect, process, and display data locally, eliminating the need for constant internet access. The AI calibration system optimizes sensor accuracy while conserving energy, allowing for extended operation and fast feedback with minimal power consumption.

_J. Safety_

Safety is enhanced by providing real-time exposure alerts, enabling users to take immediate action when air quality becomes hazardous. The monitor protects privacy by processing and storing all data locally, reducing risks associated with external data sharing or cloud storage.

_K. Compatibility_

The monitor integrates smoothly with multiple platforms, including smartphones and desktop systems, for flexible data viewing. Its universal connectivity ensures that users across different technical backgrounds can easily sync, interpret, and store their air-quality information without compatibility issues.

VI. ENGINEERING SPECS

_A. Core Components_

**PM Sensor - SEN55**

The SEN55 module measures PM1, PM2.5, PM4, and PM10, along with VOC and NOx indices (1-500), temperature, and relative humidity \[1\], \[2\]. Its particulate precision is ±5 µg/m³ or ±5% mV from 0-100 µg/m³, and ±10% mV from 100-1000 µg/m³, with PM2.5 calibrated to the TSI DustTrak™ DRX 8533 (Ambient Mode). Temperature accuracy is ±0.5 °C within 10-30 °C at 50% RH, while humidity accuracy is ±4.5% RH in the 30-70% RH range at 25 °C. The sensor incorporates a STAR-engine thermal compensation system, providing 2-3× faster thermal stabilization compared to ambient settling \[2\], \[4\]. Communication is handled via I²C at 100 kbit/s using address 0x69 with 100 Ω pull-ups \[1\], and the module operates from a 5 V supply, providing new readings approximately every second. Its compact form factor measures 52.8 × 43.6 × 22.3 mm and weighs 38.4 g \[1\]. Example environmental classifications include PM2.5 thresholds (Good: 0-9 µg/m³; Moderate: 9.1-35.4; Unhealthy: 55.5-125.4) \[10\] and VOC categories ranging from low (0-500 ppb) to high (>1500 ppb). Field evaluations have demonstrated the SEN55's strong stability in ESP32-based IoT and solar-powered deployments \[2\], and recent studies confirm that thermal compensation is essential to reduce PM bias in dynamic temperature conditions \[4\].

**Micro-controller - ESP32-S3**

The ESP32-S3 features a dual-core MCU with sufficient RAM to support TinyML workloads, along with Wi-Fi and Bluetooth LE for data syncing and OTA firmware updates. It supports FreeRTOS and TensorFlow Lite Micro for embedded AI applications, enabling localized inference without cloud dependence. The microcontroller manages sensor data acquisition, buffering, ML inference, and power-state transitions, typically waking at one-minute intervals before returning to sleep mode. Designed for compact integrations under 3 in², the ESP32-S3 offers robust TinyML performance and reliable real-time wireless connectivity, making it an effective companion to the SEN55 in edge-processing systems \[15\].

**Battery & Power Circuit**

The power subsystem is built around a rechargeable Li-ion battery, selected to provide at least 12 hours of continuous operation. System efficiency comes from a sampling strategy in which the SEN55 operates briefly (1-10 seconds) before the MCU processes the data and re-enters sleep mode. Data is aggregated at one-minute intervals, a strategy validated in prior work employing Random Forest and Support Vector Regression models \[4\], \[13\]. Calibration and performance verification will occur within the Cal Poly Air Measurements Lab, where chamber-based testing remains the gold standard for assessing sensor drift, response, and linearity \[7\].

**Communication**

Communication is handled through BLE for low-power local connectivity and Wi-Fi for extended-range synchronization. BLE employs Adaptive Frequency Hopping (AFH) to avoid interference in the 2.4 GHz band. Together, these interfaces support real-time data streaming, alerts, and wireless firmware updates.

**AI Model (Edge Calibration)**

The on-device AI model provides classification and self-calibration for PM and VOC levels, enabling reliable operation in dynamic field environments where external calibration is not practical \[3\], \[11\]. The system employs lightweight TinyML models-such as Random Forest, Support Vector Regression, or compact neural networks with 1-2 hidden layers-to fit within microcontroller compute and memory constraints \[4\]. Larger frameworks such as PyTorch are avoided due to excessive resource demands. Calibration strategies follow hybrid neural scaling and differential correction techniques, allowing the system to correct drift and environmental variation in real time \[11\], \[12\]. The EEATC (Estimated Error Augmented Two-phase Calibration) model developed by Narayana et al. \[3\] directly informs our approach, as it consistently outperforms single-phase linear and Random Forest calibration models. Data processing uses rolling temporal windows (e.g., 60-second histories) incorporating features such as temperature, humidity, and pollutant trends \[6\], and adaptivity is maintained through incremental retraining methods, including polynomial correction \[5\] and temporal architectures such as 1D-CNNs and LSTMs for complex pollutant patterns \[13\]. All inference is deployed on the ESP32-S3 using TensorFlow Lite Micro, minimizing latency and power consumption while maintaining accuracy comparable to cloud-based calibration frameworks \[6\], \[15\]. Recent literature shows that neural surrogate and hybrid ML calibration techniques substantially improve measurement accuracy for low-cost sensors, validating our edge-AI integration strategy \[6\], \[12\].

**Enclosure**

The enclosure is sized around the SEN55 and battery pack, measuring roughly 3 × 3 inches with a thickness under 2 inches. It incorporates ventilated pathways to maintain airflow and ensure sensor response accuracy, and uses lightweight yet durable materials suited for field or wearable operation. Mounting options include clip and strap mechanisms, and internal layout considerations ensure heat-producing components are isolated while airflow channels remain unobstructed.

**Overall Comments**

The combination of the SEN55 sensor and ESP32-S3 microcontroller meets the core project requirements for precision, low power, and real-time data processing. By leveraging edge-AI calibration and validated sensor architectures \[2\], \[3\], \[7\], \[15\], the system achieves high accuracy in dynamic environments while maintaining portability and user accessibility.

_B. Cost Analysis_

The estimated total cost of the device is approximately \$85, placing the wearable well under project's \$100 target price and significantly below the cost of commercial air-quality monitors. The SEN55 sensor and ESP32-S3 microcontroller represent the majority of the cost but are essential to achieving high measurement accuracy and real-time calibration. The enclosure, PCB, and battery add modest additional cost while enabling manufacturable, wearable-grade assembly. Because all computation occurs on-device, there are no continuing operational or cloud-service costs. These results confirm that the proposed design is not only technically feasible but also economically aligned with market expectations for low-cost personal sensing devices.

VIII. PROJECT TIMELINE

_A. Gantt Chart_

The full Gantt chart can be found in the appendix. Most notably, the winter quarter ranges from January 6<sup>th</sup> to March 14<sup>th</sup>, which is when the development and building of the device will occur. During this time, three phases will occur concurrently: hardware development, software development, and AI model production. In hardware development: sensors will be interfaced with hardware, status indicators and displays will be made on PCB, and a case and enclosure will be made. In terms of software development: an app will be produced on android, a Bluetooth interface will be tested between the app and the microcontroller, and code will be developed to interface with sensors for AI model training. Next, the AI model will be developed by acquiring data from lab equipment, modeling a neural network in PyTorch, and finetuning the model. Then, during Spring quarter, which is from April 1<sup>st</sup> to June 13<sup>th</sup>, final touches will be made, and any remaining errors will be fixed, as the senior project report is being finished.

IX. METHODOLOGY

Our team plans to obtain access to the Hal Cota Air quality monitoring lab, which is located at 13-201 of Cal Poly. The lab provides access to PM 2.5, PM 10, NOx, and other highly accurate air quality monitoring equipment. To determine our accuracy of the provided laboratory PM sensors, datasheets will be analyzed, and a model will be formed around them. In the case that the datasheets are not adequate, a Kalman filter will be used to obtain Covariance matrices. Additionally, a widely used model to fit data trends in a way that makes quantifying error trivial is to use orthogonal polynomials such as Chebyshev or to use a vectorized approach such as Least Mean Squares \[7\]. These approaches can be used to train the model in conjunction with Cross-Entropy Classification (Logistic Regression) and Mean Squared Error loss (Linear Regression), respectively. This training will be done through a version of gradient descent, parameter updates to adjust weights, and through repetition. Different AI models will provide different advantages, thus metrics such as model drift, R squared, and the confusion matrix will provide deeper insight into the model's effectiveness. By assessing the R squared value that the AI model has in conjunction with the measurement equipment, this value can be compared to other published data to determine the effectiveness of our calibration model.

X. TEAM'S WORK

Our work combined a structured project plan with an evidence-driven research process. In weeks 1-2, we established a detailed work breakdown structure, delegated primary tasks, and defined individual leadership areas to ensure clear ownership, accountability, and an efficient workflow for the full project life cycle. Guided by the literature on low-cost sensing and edge-AI calibration, we synthesized methods addressing calibration drift and cross-sensitivity (e.g., ensemble/Random Forest and EEATC-style approaches), which informed our ESP32-S3 + SEN55 architecture, minute-level sampling with thermal compensation, and TinyML inference on rolling windows. We then mapped these findings into testable engineering specifications and a validation methodology using reference instruments, Kalman/least-squares modeling, and metrics such as R², confusion matrices, and error relative to standards to quantify accuracy and stability. This alignment between front-end planning, research synthesis, and measurement protocol ensured a cohesive, reproducible, and standards-aware development process

XI. CONCLUSION

The wearable air quality monitoring device with embedded AI represents more than just a technical prototype - it aims to make accurate air quality awareness a part of daily life. By combining a high-precision environmental sensor (SEN55), an efficient ESP32-S3 microcontroller, and an embedded AI calibration system, our product transforms professional-grade sensing into a compact wearable form. Our device will per-form all processing locally, offering real-time responsiveness and data privacy. This autonomy allows users to continuously monitor their environment without dependence on network connectivity, making the system practical for both personal and field-based applications.

Current literature on air quality monitoring systems - from wearable PM sensors \[16\] to AI calibrated sensors - reveals the need for an innovative combination of both. Integrating the accuracy of advanced ML calibration frameworks \[3\], \[11\], and \[12\] with the portability and affordability of embedded edge computing \[15\] represents a step forward for consumer-level air monitoring systems. This gap in accurate, yet portable air quality calibration has motivated the creation of the Sensorian SEN55 - an explorative approach for a more effective way of increasing sensor accuracy in dynamic real-world environments. By addressing calibration drift, environmental interference, and the lack of accessibility found in existing systems, our device delivers a practical solution to real world monitoring challenges.

Our research verifies the feasibility of our product to compete with current state-of-the-art research \[6\], \[7\], \[12\]. A long battery life exceeding twelve hours, rapid and precise calibration within 0.2 standard deviations of known values, and a small ergonomic form factor are key important design requirements we hope to achieve. Air-quality monitoring devices are an exciting emerging technology that requires further development to see greater adoption by the public. This research helps to bridge the gap that has stopped the production of consumer products in the past. Looking ahead, our team plans to validate our device's performance through laboratory calibration and outdoor testing, ensuring that the device maintains consistent accuracy across diverse environments.

Our prototype, leveraging the SEN55 and ESP32-S3 plat-forms, builds on proven calibration strategies from recent literature \[2\], \[4\], \[6\], which validates that reliable, wearable air quality monitoring can now be achieved with minimal power consumption while maintaining high data integrity. Ultimately, our team envisions this device contributing to broader environmental awareness, encouraging healthier behaviors, and promoting data-driven environmental policies.
